1.sense: The first command given to a man who could not read, and it does not say what to read. It says under whose name to read, and it identifies that Lord by the one act nobody can claim a share in.

notes.t: Aisha's account of how revelation began has the angel take hold of the Prophet ﷺ in the cave of Hira and press him until he could bear no more, three times, each time saying read, each time answered that he was not a reader, and then giving him these opening verses.
Iqra is left without an object, which is why the tradition reads it as a command to receive and repeat rather than to decipher a page. Nothing was in front of him to look at.

The great majority hold that the first five verses of this surah are the first revelation. A minority named al-Muddaththir or al-Fatiha instead, usually by reading those reports as being about the first revelation after the pause rather than the first of all.
notes.src: the reports are collected and weighed in the commentaries and in the works on the sciences of the Qur'an

links.why: the surah the minority position names as first, and the summons that came after the pause
another opening command tied to the name of the Lord

2.sense: The verb of the previous line is repeated and then narrowed. He created, and out of everything He created the one instance named is the person being addressed, traced back to something that hangs on to a wall.

notes.t: Alaq is a collective noun from the root -l-q, to cling or be suspended. The lexicons use it of a leech, of clotted blood, and of anything that attaches itself. All three senses describe a thing that holds on to something bigger than itself in order to exist.

The order is deliberate. The creation of everything is stated first, then the creation of one species, then the state that species started from. A man told to read is being told what he was before he had eyes.
The Qur'an lays out the sequence elsewhere, from dust, then a drop, then an alaqah, then a lump of flesh, and it does so in order to argue about resurrection rather than about biology.

links.why: the same stage named inside the full sequence
the stages again, ending in another creation entirely

3.sense: The command comes a second time, to a man who has just said he cannot do it. The reassurance attached to it is not that he is able but that the One asking is the most generous there is.

notes.t: The first command was grounded in creation and the second in generosity, and the next two verses define that generosity as teaching. In this surah the most generous thing said about the Lord is that He gives knowledge.
Al-akram is the superlative of karam, which in Arabic covers giving freely, being noble in origin, and being above pettiness. The definite article makes it a class of one.
The Qur'an addresses the same worry directly in another surah, telling the Prophet ﷺ that He will make him recite and he will not forget.

links.why: the promise that the reciting will be supplied and retained
the gathering of it and the reciting of it taken as a responsibility by the One who sent it

4.sense: The generosity is spelled out and it turns out to be instruction, and the instrument named is the pen. Writing is treated here as something handed down rather than something worked out.

notes.t: A revelation given to a man who did not write opens by naming the pen. The Qur'an is not against literacy in the mouth of an unlettered messenger, it credits literacy to the same source as the message.
A qalam is a cut reed. The word is the name of a tool, so the verse credits the Lord with teaching through a thing, which is how most human knowledge actually arrives.
Another surah opens with an oath by the pen and by what they inscribe, and it does so at the point where the Prophet ﷺ was being called mad.

links.why: an oath sworn by the pen and by what it writes
the messenger described as unlettered, in the books the literate held

5.sense: The whole of what a person knows is placed on one side of a line, and the side it is placed on is the side of things received. He knew nothing, then he knew, and the change came from outside him.

notes.t: The sentence is built so that the verb taught brackets the man on both sides, allama al-insana ma lam yalam. Even the not knowing is stated in the same breath as the teaching, so there is no interval in which he was self-taught.
These first five verses say nothing about law, punishment or the hereafter. They establish who created and who taught, and the rest of the surah then deals with a man who forgot both.
The Qur'an makes the same claim about the beginning of a human life, that He brought you out of your mothers' wombs knowing nothing and then gave you hearing, sight and hearts.

links.why: the first man taught the names, and the teaching being what set him apart
the state of knowing nothing named as the starting point

6.sense: The tone turns at one word. Everything up to here has been about a gift, and from here it is about what the same creature does with the gift once he has it.

notes.t: Kalla is a word of refusal, and it is spoken to something not written in the verse. It answers an attitude rather than a sentence, which is why the surah can pivot on it without quoting anyone first.
Tugha is the verb behind taghut and behind the description of a flood that broke its banks. It is not sin in general, it is overflow, a thing going past the edge it was given.
The Qur'an uses the same verb of Pharaoh when Musa is sent to him, saying go to Pharaoh, he has transgressed, which fixes the word to a specific kind of ruler rather than a private failing.

links.why: the same verb used of Pharaoh at the moment Musa is sent
the peoples who transgressed in the lands and multiplied corruption

7.sense: The cause is given in three words. He looks at himself and concludes he is beyond needing anything, and everything in the previous verse follows from that conclusion.

notes.t: Istaghna is a form that means to consider oneself free of need. The Qur'an does not say he became free of need, which is impossible, it says he treated himself as though he were. The error is in the seeing.
The verse says he sees himself, not that others see him. Nobody had to agree with him for the transgression to start.
The Qur'an addresses the same illusion directly, telling people they are the ones in need of Allah while He is the one free of need and praiseworthy.

links.why: the direct statement of who actually needs whom
the one who withholds and thinks himself self-sufficient

8.sense: One line settles the matter without argument. The man who thinks he needs nobody is going back to somebody, and the direction of travel is stated as a fact rather than a threat.

notes.t: The address switches. The transgressor is spoken about in the third person, and this verse is said to the Prophet ﷺ, your Lord. The one who was told to read is being reassured while the other is being described.

Ar-rujaa is a verbal noun with the definite article, so it is the returning as such, not one particular trip. The phrase puts the destination first, ila rabbika, which in Arabic restricts it: to your Lord and to nowhere else.
The Qur'an states the same thing in another surah with a different noun, that to your Lord is the finality.

links.why: the same statement of where everything terminates
the end point of the hour placed with the Lord alone

9.sense: A specific person is pointed at and not named. The Qur'an describes him only by what he does, which is to stand between somebody else and an act of worship.

notes.t: Araayta is used in Arabic to make a listener look at a case and judge it. It is closer to consider this man than to did you notice him, and it is repeated three times across the next five verses.
Yanha is in the present tense, so the forbidding is a standing habit rather than one incident. The man is defined by an activity he keeps up.

The exegetes identify the man as Abu Jahl, and the reports around these verses attach to him, but the Qur'an itself withholds the name, which leaves the description free to fit whoever else does the same thing.
notes.src: the identification is in the commentaries and in reports; the text names nobody

links.why: those who bar people from the sacred mosque and from the path of Allah
the ones obstructing at the sanctuary who were never its guardians

10.sense: The object of the forbidding arrives one verse late, and it is not a rebel or an army. It is a servant, at the moment he prays, doing the one thing a servant is for.

notes.t: The Prophet ﷺ is called abd here, a servant, and not a messenger. The title strips the confrontation down to its bones: a creature turning to his Lord, and another creature telling him to stop.

The report tied to these verses is that Abu Jahl swore he would put his foot on the Prophet ﷺ's ﷺ neck if he saw him praying at the Kaaba, and when he moved to do it he backed away saying that between them was a trench of fire and something terrible and wings.
notes.src: Muslim, from Abu Hurayra, in the Book of the Description of the Day of Resurrection

notes.t: Abdan is indefinite, a servant, so the verse is not restricted to one man being stopped on one morning. Anyone forbidding anyone from prayer walks into this sentence.

links.why: instructions about how loudly to pray, given in a setting of hostility
the servant of Allah standing to call on Him, and the crowd pressing around him

11.sense: The question turns to the man being forbidden. Suppose he is on guidance. The sentence is left hanging without its conclusion, and the listener has to finish it.

notes.t: The apodosis is not stated. Arabic allows the answer of a conditional to be dropped when it is obvious, and dropping it here forces the hearer to say the damning part himself.
Ala al-huda uses the preposition of resting on top of something. In the Qur'an guidance is a surface a person stands on and error is a thing he sinks into, and the prepositions keep that distinction.
The Qur'an elsewhere puts the same either-or to opponents without deciding it in the sentence, saying that one of the two parties is on guidance or in clear error.

links.why: the same undecided pairing put to opponents as a challenge
whether anyone can guide one who is set on blindness

12.sense: A second possibility is added to the first. Not only might the man being stopped be on guidance himself, he might also be telling others to be careful of their Lord, which makes the interference wider than one prayer.

notes.t: The pair is exact. Being on guidance is what a person is, enjoining taqwa is what he does to others, so the two clauses cover his private and his public standing, and the forbidder is attacking both.
Taqwa is built on wiqayah, shielding. It is the care a person takes to keep something between himself and harm, which is why the word resists being flattened into fear.
The Qur'an gives the same instruction to the Prophet ﷺ about his own household, to enjoin the prayer on them and be steadfast in it.

links.why: the same act of enjoining, aimed at the people closest to you
a group calling to good and enjoining what is right

13.sense: The camera turns back to the forbidder. Suppose the one doing the stopping is himself a denier who has walked off. Again the conclusion is withheld, and again it is not hard to supply.

notes.t: Two verbs, and they are in the right order. Denying is a decision made inside, turning away is what the body does afterwards, so the verse traces the belief into the motion.

The third araayta has changed subject without warning. Verses eleven and twelve were about the man praying and this one is about the man interfering, which puts the two of them side by side and lets the listener weigh them.
The Qur'an uses the identical pair of verbs of the man who neither confirmed nor prayed, but denied and turned away and then went off to his family swaggering.

links.why: the same two verbs, with the walk home added
the one who denied and turned away, and what is prepared for him

14.sense: The three suppositions end in one question, and it is about knowledge rather than about punishment. The man is not told what will happen to him. He is asked whether he understood that he was being watched the whole time.

notes.t: The verb is left without an object. Allah sees, full stop, rather than Allah sees him or Allah sees what he does. Leaving it open makes the seeing a permanent condition rather than an act aimed at one person.
This is the same charge Surah al-Balad brings against a different man, who supposed that nobody had seen him. In both places the correction is a question rather than a sentence.
The Qur'an states the case in general terms elsewhere, that no three converse privately without Him being the fourth of them, wherever they may be.

links.why: the identical assumption of being unobserved, in another surah
the general statement that no private meeting is private

words.g: We will surely seize and drag

15.sense: The second refusal, and this time a consequence follows it. If he will not stop, he will be taken by the hair at the front of his head, which is how a struggling animal is controlled and how a man is humiliated in public.

notes.t: Safaa means to grip something and pull it hard, and the lexicons also carry a sense of scorching that leaves a mark. The word is physical and it is the opposite of a summons.

Lanasfaan is written with a light nun of emphasis that appears in the Mushaf as a tanwin at the end of the verb. It is one of only a few places in the Qur'an where this form is used, and it makes the threat a sworn one.
The verse says if he does not stop, not when he is judged. The door is left open for the man to change while he is still alive, and the report about Abu Jahl records that he did not.

links.why: no creature moves except that He holds it by its forelock
the guilty recognised and taken by the forelocks and the feet

16.sense: The forelock is described with two qualities that belong to the man and not to his hair. Lying and wrongdoing are attached to the part of him that is about to be gripped.

notes.t: Hair does not lie. Arabic can carry a person's quality across to a part of him, and doing it here means the hand closes on the man at the exact point his lying was decided, which the Arabs took to be behind the forehead.
The two adjectives split the offence. Kadhibah is saying what is not so, khatiah is doing what should not be done, so the description covers his tongue and his conduct without repeating itself.
The verse repeats nasiyah as an indefinite noun straight after the definite one in the line before, which in Arabic reopens the word in order to describe it. It reads as a hand pausing on the grip.

links.why: the seizing by forelocks named in the same physical terms
Pharaoh and those before him, and the sin the same root names

17.sense: He is invited to send for his people. The verse does not say he has nobody. It says go ahead and call them, which is a harder answer than saying you are alone.

notes.t: A nadi is the gathering place where the men of a clan sat and decisions were made, and Mecca had a famous one, Dar an-Nadwah, next to the sanctuary. The verse points at real furniture in the listener's city.
The command form here is not permission. Arabic uses the imperative to challenge, the way go on then is used in English, and the following verse supplies the answer to the challenge.
The Qur'an uses the same word of the people of Lut, who are charged with committing what is objectionable in their gathering.

links.why: the same word for a council, used of a group that did wrong together
a group saying we are an assembly that will win, and the reply to it

18.sense: The answer to the challenge uses the same verb. He calls his council, and the reply calls something else, and the sentence puts the two summonses in exactly matched language.

notes.t: Zabaniyah occurs only here in the Qur'an. Its root carries pushing and shoving something away with force, so the name describes what they do rather than telling you what they look like.
Sanadu is written in the Mushaf without the final waw of the verb, matching the shortened spelling of falyadu in the verse before, so the two calls look alike on the page as well as in sound.
The Qur'an describes the angels set over the Fire in another place as harsh and severe, who do not disobey Allah in what He commands them and who do what they are ordered.

links.why: the description of who is over the Fire and how they take orders
the guardians of the Fire, and their number given as a test

19.sense: The last word goes to the man who was being stopped, not to the man doing the stopping. He is told to ignore him, to put his face on the ground, and to come closer, which is the exact act the whole quarrel was about.

notes.t: Reciting this verse is a place of prostration, and it is one of the positions in the Qur'an that all the schools agree on. Abu Hurayra reported that they prostrated with the Prophet ﷺ at Idha as-samau inshaqqat and at Iqra bismi rabbik.

The Prophet ﷺ said that the closest a servant is to his Lord is while he is prostrating, and told them to make much supplication then. The order of the two commands here, prostrate and then draw near, matches that.

Kalla appears three times in this surah, at verse six, verse fifteen and here, and each one throws out a different claim: that man is self-sufficient, that the threat is empty, and that the obstruction should be heeded. The surah is built on those three refusals.

links.why: the prayer he was forbidden, now commanded in the last line
the instruction not to obey a sinner or an ungrateful one among them
